claims.text: The starting NbMoTaW alloy is equal-atomic.
The starting NbMoTaW alloy is single-phase BCC.
Untreated NbMoTaW has excellent mechanical performance up to 1600 °C.
Untreated NbMoTaW has poor room-temperature ductility.
The irradiation resistance of NbMoTaW has mainly been inferred computationally rather than established experimentally.
Warm rolling followed by low-temperature annealing will produce a sub-micron grain structure in NbMoTaW.
Warm rolling followed by low-temperature annealing will produce a high density of nanotwins in BCC NbMoTaW.
The introduced nanotwins will act as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
The introduced nanotwins will facilitate dislocation motion at room temperature.
Facilitated dislocation motion will improve the room-temperature ductility of NbMoTaW.
Nanotwins will capture and promote recombination of irradiation-induced defects.
The thermomechanical treatment will preserve the overall BCC lattice.
Preservation of the BCC lattice will support retention of high-temperature mechanical strength.
Treated NbMoTaW will have significantly greater room-temperature ductility than untreated NbMoTaW.
Treated NbMoTaW will exhibit less irradiation-induced amorphization than untreated NbMoTaW.
Treated NbMoTaW will exhibit less irradiation-induced blistering than untreated NbMoTaW.
The treatment will maintain NbMoTaW's high-temperature mechanical performance over 800–1600 °C.
The proposed irradiation benefit applies under helium implantation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires improved ductility, reduced irradiation damage, and retained high-temperature strength, but the stated rule requires simultaneous failure of both ductility and irradiation improvements while strength remains comparable. Thus, loss of high-temperature strength or failure of only one claimed benefit would contradict the prediction without satisfying the stated falsification rule.
